FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'received' AND units > 13

1. Start with a short scope note identifying the intake cycle and explaining that the figures are grouped by depot.
2. Present the received-unit totals by depot, using the results of the supplied query. If the results are not provided, leave the numerical totals unstated rather than deriving them from incomplete information.
3. Add a brief coverage note describing the status and unit-threshold filters, including the treatment of deliveries at exactly 13 units.
4. Identify any source limitations that affect interpretation, such as missing depot names or absent explanations for non-received statuses, only when those limitations are actually present in the supplied material.

Summing units does not establish how many separate delivery records were received, and the number of rows should not be described as the number of vehicles, suppliers, or arrival events unless the records explicitly support that statement. If the source includes a separate delivery count, label it separately and state which rows that count covers. If no such count is supplied, do not add one. When comparing depots, use only comparisons supported by the returned totals and make the comparison’s scope explicit. A depot with a larger total in this filtered query has more units among the included rows; that alone does not establish that it received more units overall, because smaller shipments and rows with other statuses are excluded. If only one depot appears, report its figure without presenting a comparison. If a depot has no qualifying rows and therefore does not appear in the query results, do not silently assign it a zero unless the supplied source or reporting rules confirm that interpretation.

Before drafting, check whether the extract’s reporting period is complete and whether its depot identifiers can be matched to names. If the period is described as incomplete, call it incomplete rather than calling it the latest completed cycle. If names are absent, retain the identifiers and note that names were not supplied. If the period or names are not specified at all, flag the missing information briefly and avoid filling the gap with an assumption. Apply these checks to the actual material provided; they are not reasons to invent additional records or to change the query.

Finish with a short, substantive note explaining how a supervisor should read the filtered totals alongside the limits of the extract. In particular, if a later operational decision depends on whether excluded rows should count toward a broader delivery total, keep that decision conditional: the supplied query alone does not answer it. Do not recommend a depot action, declare a result approved, or claim that a discrepancy has been resolved unless the source material explicitly supports that conclusion. Keep the final note within the stated scope and do not add a separate conclusion that goes beyond the recorded delivery data.

The irrigation repair at Alder Ridge Orchard began on May 14, after a pressure check showed that the north block was losing water between the filter station and the first lateral. The block contains 18 acres of mature pear trees, arranged in twelve rows. Each row is served by a drip line connected to a buried polyethylene main. The loss was most noticeable during the morning run, when the pump was operating at its usual setting but the far-end gauges remained below their normal range. Orchard manager Lena Ortiz asked the crew to identify the source before changing the watering schedule, since the trees were entering an important stage of fruit development.

The crew first isolated the north block at its valve and checked the filter, pressure regulator, and visible fittings. The filter screen was clean, and the regulator held steady at 32 psi. A shallow wet area beside Row 7 narrowed the search, but it did not identify the failed component. Irrigation technician Marcus Bell said, “The pressure pattern points us toward the main, but we should confirm it before we dig.” The crew recorded gauge readings at the filter station, the midpoint, and the end of Row 7, then compared them with readings from the adjacent block, which was operating normally.

A listening check and a small test excavation found a split in the main beneath the service track. The damaged section was about 40 centimeters long, with a longitudinal crack near an older compression coupling. Soil had entered the opening, and water had carried fine sediment into the low point downstream. The crew marked the location and shut off the block’s supply. Before cutting the pipe, they confirmed that the line was fully depressurized and that the valve serving the neighboring block remained closed. This separation prevented the repair work from interrupting irrigation to the other rows.

The existing pipe was 63-millimeter polyethylene, and the replacement piece came from the orchard’s maintenance stock. Bell checked the pipe rating and outside diameter against the damaged section, then inspected the new compression couplings for cracked nuts or distorted seals. The crew removed the split section with a square cut, cleaned the pipe ends, and checked that neither end had ovalized under the weight of the track. They also flushed the exposed line at low flow into a collection tub until the water ran clear. The collected sediment was bagged for disposal rather than left beside the trench.

The repair plan was recorded in the work log before the line was reassembled:
1. Keep the north-block valve closed while removing the damaged pipe and cleaning the cut ends.
2. Install the replacement piece with the manufacturer’s insertion marks visible at each coupling, and tighten the nuts by hand before using the strap wrench.
3. Support the repaired main on compacted bedding so that the coupling joints do not carry the weight of the pipe or the service track.
4. Reopen the valve gradually, inspect both joints for leakage, and compare pressure readings at the filter station, midpoint, and Row 7 end.
5. If either joint seeps or the far-end pressure remains below the adjacent block’s reading, close the valve and inspect the alignment and seals before returning the block to its normal schedule.

The crew followed the sequence and reopened the valve in stages. No water appeared around the couplings during the initial inspection. The gauges showed 32 psi at the filter station, 29 psi at the midpoint, and 27 psi at the end of Row 7. Those readings were consistent with the adjacent block under the same pump setting. After the first ten minutes, the crew checked the joints again and found them dry. Ortiz noted that the readings were useful only while the pump and neighboring block were operating under comparable conditions, so the technician recorded the pump setting and the time beside each measurement.

The line was left under observation for the remainder of the morning run. A crew member walked the service track and the first three laterals in Row 7, looking for fresh wet soil, displaced emitters, or uneven flow. None was observed. The test excavation was backfilled in compacted layers, and the surface was restored without placing loose soil over the coupling location. A small marker was set beside the track so that maintenance staff could find the repair without driving over it. The work log also included the pipe size, coupling type, repair location, pressure readings, and names of the staff who performed the inspection.

Ortiz asked the crew to keep the north block on its existing schedule for the next two irrigation cycles and to check the marked location after each run. If pressure at the end of Row 7 falls below the recorded 27 psi while the pump is at the same setting, the crew will repeat the three-point gauge check before changing the schedule. If the readings remain within the recorded range and the soil stays dry, the block will continue on its current schedule while the routine weekly inspection proceeds. Ortiz said, “I want the follow-up to tell us whether the repair is holding under normal use, not just while everyone is standing beside the trench.” The next inspection was entered on the maintenance calendar for May 16.
